aspectTitle: Pure-decoration exemption misjudged: genuinely decorative low-contrast text (must be EXEMPT) vs. meaningful text the author treated as decoration (must MEET contrast)
aspectDescription: SC 1.4.3 exempts text that is 'pure decoration' / 'decorative and conveys no information.' Understanding's test is semantic: text is decorative only if 'random words... could be rearranged or substituted without changing meaning.' Trusted Tester says to EXCLUDE text that is 'purely decorative and not meaningful (no functionality).' Deciding whether a faint watermark, ghost number, or faded divider conveys information is a meaning judgment a contrast checker cannot make. Two opposite human-judgment traps exist: (1) FALSE POSITIVE — genuine decoration (a mood word, an ornamental repeating glyph)
scenario: Legal document viewer renders a Master Services Agreement with a tiled, rotated, light-gray repeating word 'DRAFT' behind the prose at ~1.56:1. The repeated word states the contract's legal status (unexecuted draft, not the signed final); the themer treats it as decorative paper texture.
mechanism: Meaningful status text styled as a decorative repeated-word background. 'DRAFT' (#cfcfcf on #ffffff = 1.56:1) conveys document status that cannot be rearranged or substituted ('FINAL','VOID') without changing meaning, so it is NOT pure decoration and must meet 4.5:1; at 1.56:1 it fails SC 1.4.3.

aspectTitle: Logotype / brand-name contrast exemption and its loss when the logotype acts as an interactive UI component
aspectDescription: 1.4.3 exempts logotypes and brand names from contrast. Trusted Tester excludes 'text that is... In logotypes (logo or brand name).' Understanding warns the exemption 'can be problematic when logos or logotypes act as user interface components (such as a link or other interactive control)' and that 'Corporate identity or brand guidelines beyond logo and logotype are not included in the exception.' Three human judgments are required and none are automatable: (a) is this low-contrast text actually a logotype/brand wordmark versus an ordinary styled heading?; (b) is the wordmark functioning as a l
scenario: B2B industrial fastener site header renders the company wordmark 'acmecorp.com' as live HTML text in brand 'fog teal' (#6ec3b6) on white at ~2.07:1. It is a bare non-interactive <span>, and a separate 'Home' nav item carries the home destination. It is a genuine logotype, so the 1.4.3 logotype exemption applies and the page conforms.
mechanism: Sub-4.5:1 text (~2.07:1, verified in headless render) that is the company logotype/brand name, which SC 1.4.3 explicitly exempts from contrast; the wordmark is a non-interactive span (not a link/button), so it is not acting as a UI component and the exemption is not eroded. This is the control case that defines where the exemption legitimately applies.

scenario: Riverside Food Bank volunteer sign-up: the primary 'Submit registration' button is greyed (#9a9a9a on #ededed ≈ 2.4:1) with class="disabled" but NO disabled attribute and a live onclick that really submits. A genuinely disabled twin ('Save draft', native disabled attr) sits beside it in the identical grey — pixel-identical, opposite exemption.

aspectTitle: Determining the EFFECTIVE background behind text when color and background come from different tree levels, inherited cascade, z-indexed overlays, or composited semi-transparent layers (F24 cascade limb)
aspectDescription: F24 fails content when a foreground color is specified without a guaranteed background (or vice versa) and stresses that 'It is not necessary that the foreground and background colors both be defined on the same element. Foreground text color is inherited from ancestor elements. If an element's background color has not been defined, the element will have a transparent background, so authors need to ensure that at least one of the element's ancestors has a defined background color.' Color may be set 'at any level in the cascade... by external stylesheets or through inheritance.' Determining wha
scenario: Vacation-rental booking card with inherited light-gray text (#9b9b9b) on a transparent, position:absolute card shifted entirely off a dark nav rail so it renders over a bright lakeside hero photo painted on <body>; a CSSOM ancestor-walk finds the dark rail (#1b1b1b) and false-passes, but the real backdrop is the bright photo (~2.8:1).
mechanism: Foreground color inherited from .copy and a background (#1b1b1b on the positioned ancestor .stage) both exist in the cascade, so F24's bare 'missing background' condition is satisfied; the defect is that the nearest declared-background ancestor is NOT the rendered backdrop. position:absolute;left:360px places the card over the bright fixed body photo, against which #9b9b9b light gray drops to ~2.8:1, below 4.5:1.

Foreground text color is inherited from ancestor elements. If an element's background color has not been defined, the element will have a transparent background, so authors need to ensure that at least one of the element's ancestors has a defined background color.' Color may be set 'at any level in the cascade... by external stylesheets or through inheritance.' Determining wha
scenario: Wellness/yoga hero with near-white text (#f3f6f4) on a translucent white 'frosted glass' overlay (rgba(255,255,255,0.4)) composited over a bright beach/sky photo; the composite is a pale panel, so the light text falls to ~1.1-1.6:1.
mechanism: The text's nearest box-tree background is .frost, whose computed value is a translucent color over a background-image. The effective backdrop is rgba(255,255,255,0.4) composited over the bright photo, yielding a light panel on which near-white text is ~1.1-1.6:1 — far below 4.5:1. A foreground and a background are both declared, so this is not a bare F24 omission; it is a composited-backdrop misjudgment.

mechanism: No in-scope text is below threshold: rest/hover/focus link states all exceed 12:1. The only sub-threshold state is :visited (~2.03:1), and Trusted Tester explicitly excludes text 'Changed to indicate it is a visited link' from the contrast requirement, so the faint visited colour is not a 1.4.3 failure.

aspectTitle: The 'text in a picture that contains significant other visual content' exemption vs. an image of text done purely to get a particular look (which is NOT exempt)
aspectDescription: 1.4.3 exempts text 'that are part of a picture that contains significant other visual content.' Understanding explains the boundary: 'This exception is intended to separate pictures that have text in them from images of text that are done to replace text in order to get a particular look. Incidental text, such as in photographs that happen to include a street sign, are not included.' Trusted Tester excludes text 'Contained within a picture that contains significant other visual content' but requires testing 'an image of text alone (or an image with text and no other significant content)' again
scenario: B2B SaaS landing page (Cohere Ledger): the hero's most prominent headline is not live text but a flat image of text exported to lock in a custom condensed display typeface. It is a plain fill plus warm-grey lettering (no other visual content) — an image-of-text-for-look, so the exemption does NOT apply. Rendered text is 3.25:1 (CSS-exact; ~3.1-3.4 measured), below 4.5:1 for normal text. The live subhead/CTA pass, so the page looks clean to a scanner while its biggest line fails.
mechanism: In-scope image of text (no significant other visual content) rendered at 3.25:1 < 4.5:1 for normal-size text; a low-vision user cannot resolve the grey-on-cream headline and, because it is an image, cannot restyle it. Verified by eyedroppering the least-contrast text pixel vs background per Trusted Tester 13.C step 4.

scenario: Travel article (Meridian Travel, 'Walking Lisbon's Baixa'): the lead photo is a street scene with significant other visual content — sky, sun, tiled buildings, roadway, a tree, pedestrians, a triumphal arch — that incidentally includes a small green 'RUA AUGUSTA' street sign whose lettering measures only ~1.5:1. The chart-like chrome tempts a reviewer to misread it as an exempt picture.

aspectDescription: 1.4.3 exempts text 'that are part of a picture that contains significant other visual content.' Understanding explains the boundary: 'This exception is intended to separate pictures that have text in them from images of text that are done to replace text in order to get a particular look. Trusted Tester excludes text 'Contained within a picture that contains significant other visual content' but requires testing 'an image of text alone (or an image with text and no other significant content)' again
scenario: Nonprofit annual report (Riverkeep Conservancy, '2025 Impact Report'): a founder pull-quote is rendered as a flat image of text (hand-serif look) on a near-white card with no significant other visual content — so it is in scope (not exempt). Lettering #888888 on #f4f2ed = 3.17:1 (CSS-exact; ~3.09 measured): below 4.5:1 for normal text but at/above 3:1 for large-scale text. The image renders large (~40px, > 24px/18pt), so the 3:1 threshold applies and it PASSES. Pass/fail cannot be decided from the number alone — the human must first judge the rendered size.
mechanism: In-scope image of text at 3.17:1; because the rendered text is large-scale (>18pt/24px), the relaxed 3:1 threshold applies and 3.17:1 meets it. Trusted Tester notes there is no tool to compare text size INSIDE an image, so a human must demonstrate large-scale to apply 3:1 — otherwise the default 4.5:1 governs and 3.17:1 would fail. Confirmed by eyedropper plus a size determination.
